MARITIME QUARTER GETS A SECOND LIFE

PORTHAVEN (14 May) — For thirty years the warehouses along Dock Road stood empty, too solid to fall down and too awkward to convert. This month the first of them reopened as the Porthaven Makers' Yard, a shared workshop for eighty small manufacturers.

The conversion was funded by a mix of city grants and rent paid in advance by future tenants — an unusual arrangement that the project's director, Ines Cardozo, says was the only way to begin. [1] "Banks wanted a finished building before they would lend, and we needed money before we could finish one," she said. [2]

Tenants pay between £180 and £600 a month depending on floor area, well below the £1,100 average for comparable industrial space in the city. [3] In exchange, they commit to a three-year lease and to opening their workshops to the public one Saturday a month.

[4] Two further warehouses are scheduled for conversion, the second of them due to open in eighteen months. Ms. Cardozo expects demand to keep outrunning supply: the Makers' Yard received more than four hundred applications for its eighty units.

title: Questions 181-185 refer to the following article and letter.
content:
TRANSIT AUTHORITY TRIMS ROUTE 42

EASTVALE (2 November) — The Eastvale Transit Authority will shorten Route 42 from 14 December, ending the service at Fenwick Interchange rather than continuing to Marley Green. The authority says the final three stops carried an average of eleven passengers a day last year, against a network average of two hundred and forty.

Riders travelling beyond Fenwick will be able to transfer to the new Route 42B minibus, which will run hourly on weekdays and every ninety minutes on Saturdays. There will be no Sunday service.

Deputy director Hana Vogel said the change would let the authority add two morning departures on Route 42 itself, where crowding has been the subject of repeated complaints. "We are moving capacity to where the passengers are," she said.

The authority held two public meetings in September. Attendance was low — nineteen people in total — a fact critics attribute to the meetings' 2 P.M. start.

To the Editor,

Your report on Route 42 repeated the transit authority's figure of eleven passengers a day without asking how it was produced.

I have used the Marley Green stop for nine years. The count was taken in the first week of August, when the packing plant that employs most of us shuts for its annual holiday. In any other week the 7:10 service alone carries fifteen to twenty of us.

I do not dispute that the two extra morning departures are needed; the buses from Fenwick are genuinely overcrowded. But the replacement minibus runs hourly, and my shift starts at 6:45 A.M. An hourly service that does not begin until seven is not a replacement — it is a removal.

As for the public meetings, I would gently point out that a two o'clock meeting on a Tuesday is not accessible to people who work shifts. That is presumably why nineteen people came.

Constance Ebele
Marley Green

★★★☆☆  "Excellent tent, one design flaw"
Reviewed by H. Okwuosa — verified purchase

Twenty-two nights in this tent across Snowdonia and the Cairngorms, including one night of sustained fifty-mile-an-hour wind on a col where I fully expected to be walking out at three in the morning. It did not move. The six guy points are not marketing.

The two doors are worth the extra two hundred grams over a single-door tent, and being able to pitch the inner on its own was genuinely useful in Spain last month.

My complaint is the zip on the left vestibule, which snagged on the storm flap from the second week and has now failed completely. Looking at the forum, I am not the first. Thank you for this, and for the detail — a col in the Cairngorms in fifty-mile-an-hour wind is exactly what the Tarn 2 was designed for.

On the vestibule zip: you are right that this has come up before. We changed the storm-flap geometry on units manufactured after March this year for precisely that reason. Tents made before that date are covered by the guarantee for this specific fault, wear or not, and we are treating it as a manufacturing issue rather than sending it to Mend.

NORDHAVEN INTERMODAL OPENS KOLVIK RAIL TERMINAL

KOLVIK, 3 May — Nordhaven Intermodal today opened its fourth inland terminal, a 24-hectare rail-served facility 40 kilometres south of the port of Aalgard.

The site has two 750-metre loading tracks and capacity for 180,000 containers a year. Shuttle trains will run to the port six days a week, removing an estimated 62,000 lorry journeys from the coastal motorway annually.

“Customers have been asking us for an inland option since 2019,” said Petra Solheim, Chief Operating Officer. “Kolvik lets a container leave the quay in the evening and be ready for collection inland before breakfast.”

Construction took 19 months and cost €114 million, of which €31 million came from a regional transport fund. Ninety-four people have been recruited. A further 40 posts will follow when the second phase, a temperature-controlled warehouse, opens next spring.

Kolvik opens — but hauliers want the gate open longer
by Marek Ostrowski, Freight Quarterly, 11 May

Regional forwarders have given a guarded welcome to the container terminal that opened at Kolvik last week. The six-day shuttle to Aalgard was widely praised; the road gate was not.

At present the gate accepts road collections between 6 A.M. and 8 P.M. only. “If a box is ready for us before breakfast, we would like to collect it before breakfast,” said Anneke Ruys, who runs a forwarding firm in Bregge. “At the moment we cannot get through the gate until the morning peak has already started.”

Ms. Solheim told Freight Quarterly that a 24-hour gate was “under review” and that any decision would rest on the volumes handled in the first two quarters of operation. She declined to give a date.

The temperature-controlled warehouse remains on schedule for next spring.

Timber returns to the city centre

By Delphine Arroyo

Until recently, an eight-storey office block in this country meant steel and concrete. That is changing. Nineteen buildings of five storeys or more framed in cross-laminated timber were completed nationally last year, against three in the year the material was first permitted at that height.

Developers give two reasons. The panels arrive cut to size, so a floor can be assembled in days rather than in weeks, and a timber frame weighs roughly a fifth of a concrete one, which cuts the cost of foundations on soft ground.

Tenants appear to have noticed. Letting agents report that timber schemes are being taken up before completion at a rate the sector has not seen for a decade.

Not everyone is persuaded. Insurers have been slow to price the risk, and several city authorities still ask for fire modelling beyond what the building code requires. “The engineering is settled,” says Ravi Mahadevan of the practice Norrland & Vale. “The paperwork is not.”

NORRLAND & VALE — Tenant priorities survey, March

412 responses from occupiers of commercial buildings completed within the last five years.

Which single factor most influenced your choice of building?

Natural light and interior finish — 34%
Rent per square metre — 29%
Distance from a transport hub — 21%
Environmental credentials — 11%
Other — 5%

Would you pay a higher rent for a building with a timber structure?

No — 44%
Yes, up to 5% more — 38%
Yes, more than 5% more — 9%
Don't know — 9%

Respondents by sector: professional services 41%, technology 27%, public bodies 18%, retail and hospitality 14%.

MEMORANDUM

To: Design team, Studio 3
From: Ravi Mahadevan
Date: 2 April
Subject: Kesselring Quay — structure

The client has asked us to price a timber frame for Kesselring Quay alongside the concrete option and to report by the end of the month.

Two things to keep in front of us. The site is reclaimed land, so anything that lightens the building helps us at foundation level, and that argument alone may carry the decision. And the letting agent means to market the upper floors well before completion, which last week's property supplement suggests is now realistic for schemes of this kind.

I would not lean on the environmental case in the client presentation. Our own survey put that factor well down the list, behind light, rent and location, and the client's board is unlikely to think differently.

Giselle, please pull the fire-modelling correspondence from the Harbour Lane job. We should assume the same authority will want it again.

Sensors move into the greenhouse
By Adaeze Nwachukwu

Until recently the tomato growers of the Vale district judged their crop as their parents had: by hand, by eye, and by walking the rows twice a day. Since March, four of the district's largest producers have been running a system that does part of that walking for them.

Built by a small firm in the regional capital, the system buries a probe every twenty metres and reports soil moisture, temperature and salinity to a screen in the packing shed. Growers set a range for each figure, and when a reading leaves that range a message is sent.

The saving is not in labour. Ola Bergström, who grows twelve hectares under glass, says his staff still walk the rows. What has changed is water. “We were irrigating on a schedule,” he said. “Now we irrigate when the soil asks for it. That has cut our use by about a fifth.”

Whether smaller growers will follow is less certain. Installation runs to roughly $9,000 per hectare, and the district's co-operative has so far declined to subsidise it.

title: Questions 157-159 refer to the following article.
content:
Slow trains, full carriages

Overnight rail travel across the continent, written off a decade ago as a relic, carried 4.1 million passengers last year — the highest figure since 2004. Three operators have added routes in the past eighteen months, and a fourth has ordered sleeping cars for delivery in 2028.

The revival is not driven by price. A berth from Kraków to Trieste costs €149 return, roughly twice the cheapest flight on the same day. Operators say their passengers are buying something else: a night that does not have to be spent in a hotel, and an arrival in the centre of the city that needs no onward transfer.

Load factors tell the story. On the Kraków-Trieste service, single-occupancy cabins sell out first and are typically booked eleven weeks ahead, while the ordinary seated carriages on the same train run at 62 percent.

The constraint is rolling stock. A sleeping car takes four years to build, and only two manufacturers on the continent still make them.

Visitor levy to fund coastal path
By Ingrid Sælen, 12 May

Kaldvik will introduce a visitor levy of €2.50 per guest per night from 1 October, the town council confirmed on Tuesday. The charge will apply to hotels, guesthouses and licensed short-term rentals, and will be collected by the operator and passed to the council each quarter.

Officials expect the levy to raise about €1.4 million in its first full year. Roughly two-thirds is earmarked for the long-delayed coastal path between the harbour and Storneset, with the remainder going to public toilets, waste collection and the summer shuttle bus.

Guests staying more than fourteen consecutive nights will be exempt from the fifteenth night onwards, as will anyone travelling for medical treatment.

Kaldvik recorded 310,000 overnight stays last year, 18 percent more than five years ago. Councillor Renata Bielawska, who chairs the tourism committee, said the town had “reached the point where visitors must contribute to the infrastructure they use”.

A consultation on the collection procedure closes on 30 June.

To the editor,

I have run a nine-room guesthouse in Kaldvik for twenty-two years, and I am not against the levy in principle. The path your article describes has been promised since before I opened, and the state of the harbour toilets is no advertisement for us. If €2.50 a night buys those things, my guests will pay it without complaint.

My objection is to who does the collecting. Under this scheme I become an unpaid tax collector: I must add the charge, decide who is exempt, hold the money and file a return four times a year. A hotel with a finance office can absorb that. I cannot, and neither can the eleven other small operators I have spoken to.

There is an obvious alternative. The council already licenses every operator in the town. Bill the levy once a year, based on the previous year's declared occupancy, and send us a single invoice. The council collects the same money and I get my evenings back.

I would urge the committee to look at this before the consultation closes.

Small Manufacturers Share the Cost of Testing

RIVERTON (14 May) — Nineteen precision-parts makers in the Riverton industrial district have formed a cooperative to buy testing equipment that none of them could justify on its own.

The group's first purchase, a computed-tomography scanner installed in a leased unit on Kilner Road, allows a finished component to be inspected internally without being cut open. [1] Members book time on the machine through a shared calendar and are billed by the hour.

“We were each sending parts to a laboratory two hundred kilometres away and waiting nine days for a report,” said Adaeze Nwachukwu, who runs a twelve-person machine shop and chairs the cooperative. “Now it is the same afternoon.” [2]

Membership costs $4,000 a year plus usage fees. [3] The cooperative estimates that a member sending forty components a year for inspection recovers the subscription within seven months.

[4] A second unit, for surface-roughness measurement, is expected before the end of the year, and the group has opened discussions with the technical institute about using the scanner for student projects two evenings a week.
